messages.content: You are a careful experimental physicist.

You are in an unfamiliar physical world. A heavy orange anchor is fixed at x = 0.000, z = 1.500 m; a light blue probe moves around it. Coordinates are sphere centres in metres, x right and z up, y = 0; the grid spacing is 0.10 m. The anchor has mass 1 kg and the probe 0.1 kg. The probe is attracted to the anchor, but the force law of this world may differ from familiar physics and may vary with distance and time.

Your goal is to learn this world well enough to foresee how new scenes will unfold. Later, without any tools, you will see new scenes and choose which image shows the probe's future position.

You may run up to 12 experiments from the menu below, one per turn, with the tool run_experiment. Each experiment places the probe to the right of the anchor at a given distance, launches it with a given velocity at a given world time, and records it at 6 equally spaced moments over the duration. The world returns an image of the panel with the probe drawn at its start and at every recorded moment, fading from faint (start) to solid (end). If the probe reaches the anchor's minimum separation or leaves the field of view, the record stops there. Before each experiment, give in the argument expected_end_m where you expect the probe to be at the end of the record ([x, z] in metres). It is recorded and not scored.

From time to time you will also be shown a new scene in this world and four candidate futures; answer with one letter, then you will see the true outcome.

Simple kinematics: x = -0.6+0.3*0.4=-0.48, z=0.6-1.1*0.4=0.16, with small pull toward anchor (up and right) curving it slightly. That's closest to minimal deviation from straight line.
